utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to greet everyone present in the courtroom. Mr. Pusic still hasn't returned, but I've been told that he should be with us on Monday. I'll be rendering a model decision that will slightly modify a previous decision rendered on the 19th of September with regard to the admissibility of an exhibit relating to the witness Islamovic. Apart from the number of the exhibit, P09701 will also be admitted, but we will withdraw from the list that I have referred to two exhibits that were not shown to the witness, Exhibit P03091 and P09863 -- 463, interpreter's correction. The last exhibit is P09463. There we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak has 30 minutes for his cross-examination today. Mr. Praljak, put your questions, and please do not plead. Put questions to the witness so that he can answer yes or no. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Pusic's Defence counsel has granted its 20 minutes to General Praljak, so that these additional 20 minutes should be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We thought that Mr. Pusic's time had already been used by Ms. Nozica. We cannot extend that time. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to inform you that I used up 10 minutes of the time that I had been granted by my colleague, colleague -- my colleague Ms. Alaburic, and 10 minutes that I'd been given by Defence counsel for Mr. Coric. So I didn't use Mr. Pusic's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could you do the necessary calculations, please. Yes, Mr. Praljak. Please go ahead. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day to everyone present.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. As you have noticed, we have severe time restrictions, so please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, as the witness has been granted protective measures, don't refer to the functions he held, the positions he held. We don't want him to be identified. If you feel it is necessary, you should request that we move into private session. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'll take care, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, please answer my questions by saying yes or no, I don't know, or I can't remember or something to that effect. Would it be correct to say that only the 18th and 19th of October, 1993, a conflict broke out between the Croats and the Bosniaks in Novi Travnik. In 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be correct to say that information spread throughout the -- the field, the information on war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the Croats claimed that it's the Bosniaks that provoked the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I received, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be correct to say that the Bosniaks claimed that the Croats had provoked the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the Muslims, the Bosniaks, claimed that the conflict in Novi Travnik had been provoked by the votes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be correct to say that of -- as of the 23rd of October -- or from the 23rd of October until the 29th of October the final conflicts were underway for Jajce, and on the 29th of October Jajce was taken by the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really tell you anything about the exact date, but I saw with my very own eyes what the situation in Konjic was. I saw the forces in Konjic that were withdrawing from Jajce, that had withdrawn from Jajce and were heading southwards.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would it be correct to say that after the fall of Jajce the Croats accused the Muslims of not having fought well enough and that it was their fault that Jajce had fallen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such information. I couldn't claim whether the information was correct because I'm -- I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would it be correct to say that the Muslims accused the Croats of not having fought well enough in Jajce, and they said that it was the Croats' fault that Jajce had fallen? Were there such rumours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So please confirm this once more. On the 23rd of October there was a conflict in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Similarly, the Croats -- or my question is, did the Croats claim that the Muslims had provoked the conflict and the Bosniaks claimed that the Croats this provoked the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can claim with full responsibility that the Croats provoked the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look, I'm asking you the following now: Did the Croats say one thing and the Muslims, the Bosniaks another thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both those statements are correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be correct to say that after the fall of Jajce about 30.000 displaced persons left Jajce, they set off from Jajce? Could the usher please put this map on the ELMO so that we can have a look at it. Could you please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the registrar has told me that when you put the question, you should turn the microphone off. You should then allow the witness to reply and then put the microphone on again. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: Were there about 15.000 to 17.000 Bosniaks who left Jajce and settled somewhere in Central Bosnia, Bugojno, Travnik, Zenica, in that wide area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they fled to those areas. I don't know whether that's the right number or whether the number was larger. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the same number or slightly smaller number of Croats passed through Central Bosnia, through Rama, during the period we're referring to, the end of October, and they went to Livno, to Croatia, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who passed through Prozor -- well, it wasn't possible for me to see them because I wasn't there, but I know for sure that they did pass through via that corridor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And there is one more question since you were involved in military matters as well. Do you know what the defence situation was after the fall of Jajce, at least as far as the breakthrough of the Serbian forces is concerned on the Travnik-Novi Travnik-Busovaca-Kiseljak and Sarajevo axis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on. Do you know that there were people who were severely wounded in Jajce, and they had been taken out by an armoured bus that came to assist them from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got any reliable information about that, but I couldn't deny what you have said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's my first series of questions, and I thank you for your brief answers. I will now move on to the second series of questions I have to put to you. This relates to what you said in your statement about my role within the context of the events in Rama. Could you please show the witness another piece of paper. Here you are. Thanks. Could you please read through this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, what is this document? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] It's a telefax. It's a fax. It's from the ABiH. And on the 25th of October, 1992, it was sent from Mostar to Igman. It's the Tactical Group 1, Konjic. We've mentioned this. And the deputy commander of the 4th Corps, Mr. Budakovic, sent it. His nickname is Tetak, and the text reads as follows -- can I read it or should the witness do so? He can control it. A message from Mostar from Tetak the Mostar Brigade. General Praljak has informed us that ABiH forces and HVO forces in the territories of the municipality of Jablanica and Konjic should move away from each other to avoid a conflict. It was conveyed to Dr. Rusmir and the staff in Konjic and Jablanica were informed of this fax.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know who Dr. Rusmir was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was the chief of the Konjic municipality. Dr. Ruzmir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Hadzihuseinovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the booth please interpret, because I'm not receiving any interpretation. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Dr. Ruzmir Hadzihuseinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the chief of the Konjic municipality, the head of the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this date, two days after the conflict in Prozor, and could we agree that I had already had meetings in Mostar and that I had requested that the units in Konjic and Jablanica move away from each other so that the conflict in Prozor wouldn't spread beyond those boundaries? That's what this text here says. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd just like to establish the date of my arrival in Rama.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just to make one thing clear, you, Mr. Witness, have answered, "That's what it says here." Does this mean that you learn about this by reading this document, or did you know so at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the contents of this document are concerned, well, I wasn't familiar with them, but I do know that there was contact at the level of the armija and the HVO so that this could be done, and so that what Mr. Praljak said could be treated as the objective or, rather, the objective was what Mr. Praljak said. They didn't want the conflict to spread beyond those boundaries. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now for my following question: You are from Rama, and you probably know -- or do you know that I went to primary school in Rama from 1951 until 1955?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you lived in Prozor, not in Rama, but that's still Prozor now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Okay. Prozor. From 1951 to 1955.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you were in Prozor, and I know that you were there because your father worked in the Ministry of the Interior at the time, in UDBA.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In UDBA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in UDBA. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. I believe that the accused have a problem. They aren't hearing the witness. There must be some technical problems. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In your statement it says but for the 29th and 30th of October I was seen in Prozor. My question is as follows: Did you ever see me in Prozor before the 29th or the 30th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now see 3D00418. Could we please have 3D00418. There it is. Please enlarge this. Could we enlarge it, the first part of it. There it is. We also have the English translation, of course, for the Judges. Do you want me to read it out or should you read it out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Aloud or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: "There is a great deal of chaos and tension from Igman-Konjic, Jablanica, Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Novi Travnik and we can see a marked change in the conduct of the HVO on the whole territory but also very murky activity amongst the ranks of the independent platoon or -- no, independent leaders as well as voids --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says "like Juka Prazina" if I can say what it says there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. "Juka Prazina MUP and everywhere -- and everywhere, in all places there are one to two independent commanders from the ranks of the army, which intensifies -- is intensifying its destructive activity."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the English be placed on the screens, please. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question to you is as follows: First of all, that there is tension. We've read that out. Then that Juka Prazina is causing problems and he has a brigade, almost an entire brigade in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Juka Prazina, for a time, was a very positive individual, but afterwards he became more of a renegade and he did and acted according to other people's instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we read the date? It is 04/11/1992, is it not? And it says that there are certain renegade commanders in all places which are intensifying their destructive action. That's what it says. Thank you. Shall I read point 4 and you can follow point 4 if I get something wrong.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can't see point 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: May we zoom in on point 4, please? "Our first meeting today was in Jablanica at 1130 hours with refugees from Prozor. We determined that about 80 Muslim houses were destroyed and torched. In addition to all these difficulties, there is a list going around of individuals who they intend to arrest or kill as soon as they return to Prozor, and these are all fighters which gave any kind of assistance, armed assistance or logistics assistance to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Prozor. We will learn the exact names tomorrow." So the situation as you said yourself in the Prozor and in the Rama municipality was not a good one, and there was certain threats, various threats, being hurled. Now, point -- we come to point 5, and Ms. Nika Pinter spoke about this yesterday. She said that in Prozor the situation was very serious and that one of the groups there that was a renegade group and escaped control was the HOS, the H-O-S. It had escaped all kinds of control.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I wasn't there I can't really say, but I had some previous information which testified to the fact that that might be possible, but I can't confirm the correctness of that because I didn't see it. I didn't experience it. So I can't say either way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, please, do you know that the HOS at the time was recognised as a regular army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have a few more points to look at here. May I look at paragraph 8 on the next page. 8, please. Yes, thank you. May we zoom in on point 8. Here it is. I'm going to read it slowly. "On several occasions the general stress that the HVO, and he respected only Izetbegovic and the Supreme Command -- he doesn't know the Supreme Command of the armed forces of BiH and expects to see Sefer Halilovic tomorrow or the following day at the meeting in Jablanica. He also emphasised that the BH army command -- that he would ask of the BH army command that they exclude certain members of the military command and that energetic measures be taken to do so, and it was evident that he was alluding to Sefer and of the lower command especially Zejnil." And in brackets it says, "Which would be a good service as far as I'm concerned says the signatory of this text. He agrees that we should solve the problem of joint commands and the schedules for them including the forward command post." Now, from this text can we see that we invested a great deal of effort to come into contact one way or another with Sefer Halilovic and that I claim that Zejnil, who was later arrested and escaped to Germany, wasn't working probably, wasn't doing good work in bringing Muslims and Croats closer together? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could accept some of those assertions. However, I don't have reliable information to the effect that Zejnil Delalic was an impediment to cooperation but I can't say that there were not obstacles on both sides and lack of trust on both sides.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Their Honours will be able to read the text for themselves, so I'd just like to read out point 11. It says: "In Jablanica where general -- where they referred to us, General Praljak said that there should be a meeting with refugees from Prozor at 2100 hours. He was calm and able to give guarantees that the relations in Prozor would be set right quickly." And then point 10: "In Gornji Vakuf the two previous commissions continued their way to Bugojno and we, Amidza and I, started out for Prozor, and a fighter who had been detained was release from Gornji Vakuf according to promises made in Vakuf." Now, do you know how many meetings I had at that time in that area in Vakuf, Jablanica, Konjic, Prozor with all parties concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the number of meetings. I don't know, but I do know that you were active during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like us to see another text on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for having to intervene, but I think there was a mistake in the translation on page 12, line 5. The witness's answer was that there was interference and lack of trust on both sides, and I think that "interference" -- the word "interference" was left out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that if an English text exists, could it be placed on the ELMO so that we could read the text that already exists. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could we have 3D00291, please. May we zoom in on the text, please. We saw in the previous document -- that the previous document claimed that the situation in the area changed. It was improving quite obviously with respect to relations between the army, et cetera. Now, can we read the report? It is probably compiled by the information service which says: "In the last few days, after General Praljak's arrival, many things in Prozor changed. General Praljak, on the 30th of December, 1999, arrives in Prozor and, immediately after his arrival, he orders the release of a group of prisoners, including Salih," and then the name. Et cetera. Now, since in your statement you speak about this extensively, what the situation was like, I'm going to ask you just two things. Do you remember that when you were in Prozor you were returned, and when they beat you up on the road towards Here and when you were insulted by a young man from HOS, do you happen to remember that I ran after that idiot with a gun in my hands and I was almost ready to shoot at him? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I remember that, but he wasn't a member of HOS. He was a member of the HVO, and I know his surname as well. I know who it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Unfortunately, I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know his name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. You said that you knew the idiot's name. Can you give us his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nikola Maric, nicknamed Nidja. He was a pupil of mine. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You know that after that conflict they collected up all the Muslims' cars and took them -- drove them off. Now, do you know that as far as a green Mercedes was concerned that belonged to a prominent Bosniak Muslim from Prozor, a prominent citizen, I seized it and returned the car to the gentleman, and that this almost caused shooting between myself and those people who against this, what I did. Do you know that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know whose car it was, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, you say if you like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want me to say, I'll say. The car belonged to Emir Delilovic. It was a Mercedes. His Mercedes was seized and a member of the HVO stormed the garage to do so. Do you know that there was -- I don't know about that but I don't doubt it. I'm sure that he was ready to do what he wanted. He wanted to prevent you from returning the car because it was big booty for him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could we look at the next document 3D00419, please. Thank you. It says here "the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Main Staff Mostar, the 6th of November, 1992." And on the right it says "To all HVO and BH army members." Now, there's quite a number of points there, and on page 2 it is signed by Major General Slobodan Praljak. There are two stamps, one which was the Joint Command. Now, do you know that at the time we invested great efforts to set up a Joint Command and that we devised a joint stamp for that too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the joint stamp, although I didn't see it, but I do know that an agreement was almost reached, but even if an agreement was reached, it was never put into practice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, from this order it has been translated and the Court can read it for itself. I'd like to read point 3. "The transport of weapons for the need of the military will be escorted by HVO and the Bosnia-Herzegovina army members." Is that what it says? "Transports of weapons for military units shall be escorted," et cetera. And under 5 it says "village watches should be formed in all villages of people outside military units and they should be issued with the necessary weapons." That's what it says; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And to issue the necessary weapons to them. Issue them the necessary weapons. Have you found that? It's in 6. In every village establish village guards composed of, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was never put into practice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I completely agree with you, sir. All I'm saying is can we agree that from this order of mine, it is evident that I know or that we know what was going to happen in the depth of the territory if the situation was allowed to develop and become worse. And this point testifies to that, and it says that it would be necessary to establish village watches in order to avoid uncontrolled, completely uncontrolled individuals and groups to do something that this Court here is going to deal with for the next three years. And do we agree that this was impossible without a Joint Command, because it would be very difficult for one side to do this itself? So do we agree that that was the intention and spirit of this point of the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the contents of this document, we can see that ways and means were sought to overcome the conflict. However, what was to happen afterwards confirmed either that you didn't have the capability of implementing it or that you gave up on it and did not implement it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to what I was and what I did at the time down there, but let's just look at another document now. I haven't got it in my hands -- or, rather, I'd like to ask the usher to hand the document to the witness for him to read out. They are two documents, the first and then the second. "Department of Defence, military police, I hereby order" -- and this is an order that all the vehicles confiscated from Prozor should be collected up, and the commander of the 2nd Battalion and the head of the traffic police, Halilovic, are charged in doing what we did as follows. Now, do you know how many confiscated vehicles were returned to the people who returned to Prozor themselves, the ones that we could reach? Do you know anything about that, any facts and figures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I think very few.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, may we zoom down. Yes. Scroll down. At the bottom here I added something to this order. It says to Colonel Zeljko Siljeg. Act upon the order. I just think that the date is wrong. It should read the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says 19th of December, by 2000 hours, to be executed by 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. But since all the documents relate to November, I think that the -- a mistake was made with the date, but can you see my signature where I order that that should be done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a signature, and I assume it's yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let's have the next document, please. This is again an order issued by Mr. Valentin Coric, the military police administration. And in this order, one of the points in my order that mixed military police be formed in Travnik and in Prozor where conflicts had erupted, here he implements it. Can we scroll down a bit. It says: "From the 5th Company of the 3rd Battalion to the intervention company for Prozor, I assign 20 military policemen to be designated by the company commander, and according to ethnic affiliation, they should be 10 Croats and 10 Muslims."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here, but it was never implemented.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you sure it was not implemented? Are you certain of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know there was no joint police, that nobody in the Bosniak command approved this or agreed to it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: There were many Muslims in the military police of the HVO. It doesn't say here that these were Muslims from Rama. There was proportional representation of Muslim Bosniaks and Croats who were all in the military police of the HVO. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who were in the HVO carried out exclusively the orders of the HVO and not any orders issued by any organ of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. The French interpretation just stopped. I would like to request again both Accused Praljak and the witness to be so kind and to slow down. They have to understand that they are somehow in a heated debate which I do not think is the right thing to do. They are not to debate each other. They have to ask questions and give answers in a calm atmosphere, and they have to take into account that there is interpretation going on, and therefore I try to ask you to follow this advice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I usually speak quite loudly when I speak, and as far as I know, so does Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we're on the topic. Can you testify that the things that occurred in Rama, according to your statement, I solved not by speaking loudly but by yelling, shouting, howling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said in my statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Whether this functioned or not we'll establish in due course. We can remove this text now. And please look at 3D00289. We were speaking about Jajce. Jajce had fallen, and there was great fear that the Serbs would cut through Central Bosnia and arrive at Sarajevo and cut Bosnia-Herzegovina completely into two parts. For this reason, a volunteer formation was sent to Jajce consisting of 400 armed soldiers who were armed in Capljina. Do you know, first of all, that among these 400 soldiers who were armed and sent to help Jajce there was 80 per cent Muslims who were volunteers from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this particular instance, but I do know that in other cases Bosniaks arrived from Croatia to fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know, and it says so here -- this is signed by myself and the head of the defence department, Mr. Stojic, and it says the following: "So far this group has been prevented twice by Muslim units from moving towards Jajce. Today, I agreed that representatives of the HVO and the SDA should go together and that they should accompany the units of the HVO and the armed forces of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to solve the problems which have arisen and that our group should be allowed to go in the direction of Jajce. Do your utmost to smooth out any disagreements with the Muslims in Novi Travnik and Fojnica and to influence the Muslims to ensure unhindered passage to Jajce from their side." Are you aware that these people were sent home and that they never actually managed to arrive and help Jajce?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were prevented, but I do know that the forces which were in Prozor were deployed from the 19th of October - I may be wrong about the precise date - until the outbreak of the conflict in Prozor. They wanted to proceed towards Jajce but were prevented from doing so. As for your question, I was unable to obtain such information in the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you aware that these are the same forces, the so-called Prkacin forces? Do you think these are the same forces or different forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they may be the same or they may be different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we now answer the following: Do you know from the 29th or 30th of October, over the following two months, I was staying in the areas of Jablanica, Konjic, Prozor, Novi Travnik, Travnik, and Busovaca, and what my role was there until Christmas 1992? Did you have any information about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had partial information. And we met once. If I'm correct about the date, it was on the 17th of November, in the museum in Jablanica. We spoke at length then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak has not switched on his microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a follow-up question. You have just said that you met General Praljak on the 17th of November. How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How was he what? I'm sorry, I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How was he dressed? What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I think -- I think I'm not wrong, I'm rarely wrong, I think he was wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he have any insignia on his uniform? Did he have any HVO insignia on his uniform? What could you see if you remember, because this was quite a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think if Mr. Praljak, when he arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina from Croatia, he was wearing HV insignia. It's more likely that he was wearing HV insignia than HVO insignia, but I couldn't swear to that. I know, however, where the gentleman came from. So I'm telling you my opinion. I didn't really pay attention at that point in time, but in my opinion it was more likely to have been an HV insignia than an HVO insignia. I'm not certain I'm right about this, however. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]. Well, I fully agree with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you say, Witness, what the problems concerning uniforms were? Very often I didn't have more than one uniform. And can you confirm that it wasn't matter of insignia but of what I could find to put on? Do you find such an idea convincing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may be your fault for not demanding that you get the appropriate uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At that point in time it didn't seem to me to be -- well, let's look at your statement. On page 3 you say, "as I wasn't a member of the Municipal Board I don't know whether the issue of illegal army was raised at the meeting of the Municipal Board." This was the arming of the HVO. Do you know that in 1991 the Security Council, consisting of permanent and non-permanent members, issued a decision that Croats and Muslim Bosniaks had no need to defend themselves against the Serbs and that they should be denied the opportunity of obtaining weapons? And from this it follows that any kind of procurement of weapons was illegal and punishable by law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is correct for more than one reason. If you want me to explain what I mean by this, I'm willing to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to say that in the question which was raised by General Praljak, it is probably in a way not a good approach. I know that you spoke about the position of Resolution of the Security Council which actually denied access of Bosnia and Herzegovina or everyone and everybody in the former Yugoslavia to get weapons. That is true. On the other hand, we have to say that in that Resolution it was never said what you've said, that is that issued a decision -- and I quote from your question, "That the Security Council issued a decision that Croats and Muslim Bosniaks had no need to defend themselves against the Serbs and that they should not -- should be denied the opportunity of obtaining weapons." This kind of sentence has never figured in the Security Council Resolution. I do not have it before me, but I am sure that it was not in that way formulated, and therefore I would like to ask you probably to refrain from this kind of opinion, which may be interpreted in the way as you did, but I do not think that it is the task of yours or ours now to judge how the Security Council decided at that time. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honours, I stand by my opinion, to which I have a right. I know what the consequences of that were, but I will not mention it any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If it is your opinion, you say, "It is my opinion that," but you cannot say the Security Council said so-and-so and then you are told, no, the Security Council did not, and then you say, "But it is my opinion." This is the difference, and I think my colleague was quite right with his observation. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was only trying to ask whether it was illegal to procure any kind of weapons in view of the Security Council Resolution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was every procurement of weapons illegal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was illegal, but under that Resolution the hands of the Bosniaks and the Croats were tied. The army had vast amount of weapons, and the year before that all the weapons of the Territorial Defence were withdrawn from the municipalities to the military depots, so that both of the Bosniaks and the Croats were unarmed, were disarmed by this. So that is exclusively the army that had more than 90 per cent of all the weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was not my intention to accuse anyone, least of all the Security Council, but such a decision had terrific consequences. It had repercussions on this whole problem of renegade groups. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it had dreadful repercussions because chaos ensued and it was very difficult to keep it under control because everything became illegal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that I arrived there on the 29th or 30th of October a few days before this to Jablanica as the assistant of the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was informed and told, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you know that -- or are you aware that anyone whether, Mate Boban or Jadranko Prlic or Bruno Stojic or anyone else ever gave me any document appointing me in charge of anything? Are you aware of me receiving any kind of document either from the Croatian authorities or the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina to do what I was doing there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about documents and decisions, but I know that we were told that you had arrived from Croatia to assist, that you had arrived in the area and that you were authorised and that your authority was greater than that of the local commanders. That was what the Bosniaks understood. I'm not saying whether you had or didn't have any such powers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your very correct reply, but you are not aware that anyone ever appointed me in charge of anything. If what I am saying is true, I was completely illegal up there throughout those two months up to Christmas. Would then this have been an illegal sojourn there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to what you say, yes. But judging by your behaviour on the territory of Prozor municipality one wouldn't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Praljak, please. Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you characterise my activity, the energy I invested as something that contributed or substantially contributed to resolving the misunderstandings and conflicts with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the 23rd of October until the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your public statements, the ones I know about, would lead to such a conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: After the 23rd, when the conflict in Rama erupted, until the end of 1992, were there any conflicts in Jablanica, Konjic, Prozor, Vakuf, Travnik, Novi Travnik or was the situation relatively good and peaceful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation might be described, conditionally speaking, as tolerable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If, then, I acted in that manner and these men here who are accused were -- or, rather, interpreter's correction. Had these accused here been opposed to this activity of mine, would they not have sent someone there to arrest me or obstruct me or ask for my authorisation and stop me from doing all this? Wouldn't that have been normal if they had disagreed with my activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally am convinced that the gentlemen you mentioned knew about your activities. That's my opinion, because if it had not been the case, you would have been removed just as some other people had been removed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one follow-up question. And could the registrar also calculate the time, please. In this period of October and November, during this period when there were visits, when such as the visits of General Praljak who was the deputy minister in Croatia, did the local media give accounts of these visits? Were there any articles published in the press that related to this subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where I was located, Mr. Praljak knows what the situation is. The others don't, or they do from hearsay information. I didn't have any access to the information or to the media. It wasn't possible for me to gain access to such information. All I know is that at that time certain media and the Croatian television, for example, caused a special kind of disturbance. Sarajevo television, Smirko Sako, that's his name. He wasn't in favour for -- of an end to the conflict. He enjoyed the opportunity of speaking about negative things rather than having to speak about positive things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you've used up 58 minutes. Ms. Pinter has taken up 10 minutes. That amounts to almost an hour and 10 minutes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I have another two brief questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On page 4, you said: "The Serbian Montenegrin forces towards the end of 1991 in the municipality of Prozor, there was an evident danger of war. The Serbian and Montenegrin forces, we call them Chetniks, arrived in Kupres. That's a municipality that borders with Prozor to the west. And you say that the Serbian and Montenegrin forces consisted of one tank unit from the area of Mostar. This unit was stopped in the area of Siroki Brijeg, because the Bosnian Croats in that area did not want to let them pass. After our President Alija Izetbegovic had interfered, the tank unit was allowed to proceed towards Kupres." Could we agree that Mr. Izetbegovic came, he was applauded, and the public described out, "Alija, Alija," and did he ask the Croats to let this tank unit through? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a fact. We could disagree but that was a fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I have only have two minutes. Do you know that that tank unit destroyed Kupres with other forces and killed scores of Croats and then attempted a breakthrough from Livno to Split? Are you aware of those two events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the second event is concerned, no, I'm not familiar with that one, but I do know that in autumn 1992 they shelled Prozor from Kupres quite frequently and a number of Croats were killed and there were a number of wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We won't even address the subject of Kupres now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there were victims in Kupres. That's well known.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And one more subquestion, a minor psychological question. Could you say how one can explain to Croats who had a lot of victims? They say, for example, we were killed by that tank unit which we let through at the request of Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I object. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'll withdraw that question. I'll withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which are not welcome here. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'll withdraw the question. Although such questions are very important because in fact they demonstrate what the essence of the matter was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: One more matter because you claim I was involved in propaganda with Siljeg. Did you hear or see that I had at anyplace or at any time in any newspapers or on radio station in Rama, after Rama, ever say anything insulting about Bosniaks or Muslims? Did I ever say anything that might provoke war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as your acts are concerned, within that context, no, I never heard anything of that kind, but on the basis of the information that we received, perhaps it was intentioned information received. But on the basis of that information you weren't referred to that frequently but I know that Siljeg was a hard-liner and it was far easier to debate matters with you rather than with Zeljko Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That you never heard me say anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you for assisting me in determining the truth. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I regret the fact that although we have an honest witness here and we're dealing with complicated matters, because that's when this war was brewing and there were efforts made with regard to this Joint Command, but I regret the fact that I don't have sufficient time to question this witness. I don't want to hold speeches or put myself in the limelight here, but I would just like to attempt to demonstrate why a different route was subsequently followed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, rest assured you will have the opportunity of calling all the witnesses you wish to hear so they can support your position. Unfortunately, we are limited by time. We'll now have another Defence team and they have 25 minutes for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25 minutes. Not 250 minutes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I forgot to put a question that Ms. Nika didn't put. Your Honours, may I put one more question to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may use my time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. My name is Vesna Alaburic. I am a lawyer from Zagreb and I represent General Milivoj Petkovic in these proceedings. I will put just a few questions to you since I only have 15 minutes, since I have granted 10 of my minutes to my colleague Ms. Nozica. Before I put my questions to you, could you just clarify something? It concerns an answer that you gave to General Praljak. When you discussed weapons and the sort of weapons that -- the army took from the Territorial Defence and when you said that 90 per cent of the weapons ended up in the hands of the army, we all know which army you have in mind, but it must be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the former JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to clarify. Thank you very much. The JNA. In your statement, you said where you were on the 22nd of October. You said that you were at the front line facing the Serbian army. This is on page 8 of the B/C/S version of your statement. It's the last passage, and it's at the beginning of the 9th page. And in the English version it's the middle of the page 8. If I may summarise what you said, you said that on the 22nd of October, you were supposed to be relieved. A shift was supposed to relieve you. This did not happen. You reported to your commander, Muharem Sabic. Your commander told you that you should leave those positions and head in the direction of Prozor. The HVO commander ordered you to hold to positions without this HVO commander being aware of the fact, and he held the neighbouring positions. You headed off in the direction of Gornji Vakuf. Have I correctly summarised what you stated about what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the basis of that statement of yours, would it be correct to draw the conclusion that on the 22nd of October you and your unit left the front line, which was no longer defended? You left the front line facing the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't leave that line. If I hadn't left the line, then, two hours later I would have been arrested, and together with that unit I would have been held hostage because the situation in Prozor had become more complicated, and the best proof of that fact is that the day after there was an attack launched in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in your Prozor [as interpreted] you mention a slightly different location but that's not important now. In your statement you said if you had remained at those positions, and I quote: "That would have meant that we wouldn't have been able to help Territorial Defence units in Prozor when the HVO started attacking Prozor." This is on page 9 of the Croatian version, and it's page 8 in the English version. As far as that is concerned, how did you, when you were leaving the front line facing the Serbian army on the 22nd of October, set off in order to help Territorial Defence units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you leave the front line or not, because initially you said no. Now Defence counsel is telling you that you left the front line. Were you at the front line or did you leave the front line? And if you did leave the front line, where did you go, on the 22nd of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 22nd -- on the 22nd of October, it was a Thursday. At about 1300 hours a shift was supposed to arrive to relieve us, a joint shift. We were up at the positions -- that we were holding four positions facing Kupres. That's the Idovac area. There were four positions where these positions were being held. No shift arrived to relieve us, but the Croats were relieved. I asked the new commander, Mr. Ante is his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Misic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Misic. He was a good friend of mine. I even knew his late father when he was a policeman because we were from a neighbouring village. I suggested to him, let's see what the situation is. I'll be relieved. We were using the same communications centre. We slept together. We were at the positions together. There's nothing usual up until then. He went to phone my commander, and he told me that Sabic had received an order and said that at 1800 hours, after the shift had been relieved, I shouldn't send a new shift. I should line up the soldiers and head towards Prozor. I'd like to thank Misic, because he said, "Professor, teacher, I've been instructed and told that you shouldn't leave here. Do not leave. I'm not allowed to leave. Don't leave, because there's the regular army two kilometres in front of Jaklica Staje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But what did you do? Witness, what did you do? Did you leave or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 1800 hours there was a vehicle with this shift. I headed off towards the position, but this person had told me that I shouldn't go down there, because if I did I would be attacked and disarmed. So as ordered by the commander Sabic, I turned the troops around and went to Voljice in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you left and headed off to Gornji Vakuf. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Voljice is the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to conclude that you reached an agreement or you were ordered by your commander Sabic to leave the front line facing the Serbian army, and you set off in the direction of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can interpret this as you will, but I followed my orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, but these were orders and that's what you did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obeyed the commander. I always obeyed my superior officers. I never disobeyed orders issued by my superiors. I did what I was ordered to do, and if someone had to suffer the consequences, the person who provoked the entire situation should have suffered the consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you went to this village, were you alone or with the soldiers who were with you? How many of you set off in the direction of this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were 30 soldiers, 32 soldiers, but I had let two of the soldiers go home. So there were 30 soldiers. We arrived in Voljice. I contacted the commander of the Municipal Staff from Gornji Vakuf, Mr. Agic. He asked me to come to Gornji Vakuf. I told him that I wouldn't get through because of the HVO. I sent my commander who was the commander of that shift in Idovac. He went to Gornji Vakuf. He established contact, and I was ordered by Mr. Agic from Gornji Vakuf, the commander of the Municipal Staff, to stay at that position until the following day, to rest there, to wait for orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to remind you of an exhibit shown to you yesterday by my colleague, Ms. Pinter. It was a criminal report filed against you. I'd just like to remind you of it, because we don't have time to analyse the contents of the report, but do you remember that a report was submitted against you because you were suspected of having committed the crime of having abandoned your combat positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, on the 30th of November, when Mr. Praljak came to Prozor with Begic to fetch me, I was arrested in the village of Pajic together with another 12 or 13 soldiers. Please, you'll be given your answer. Then Mr. Begic and Mr. Praljak reached an agreement. They had reached an agreement earlier on. Mr. Praljak convoyed an order to me --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I really have very little time. That is not the answer I want.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another minute, you'll receive your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I just want to know whether you can confirm that a criminal report was filed because you were suspected of having committed the crime of abandoning your combat position. That's all I'm interested in right now. If you can't remember the contents of the criminal report, we'll move on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never read it, nor did I receive it, but on that day when Mr. Praljak ordered that I be released and that I should bring 30 men from villages to normalise the situation. Well, that's what happened. The gentleman arrived. He said, "A report has been drafted. We have to take him to Grude so that he can be heard." Mr. Praljak exploded and told him, "Sir, I'm in command here. You aren't."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's not necessary to repeat that. I think the report, the criminal report concerned that crime. What I'm more interested in is one of your sentences. You left the front line facing the Serbian army. You set off in another direction. And in your report it says -- in your statement it says this meant that we wouldn't be able to help the Territorial Defence units in Prozor when the HVO launched an attack on Prozor. Please tell us how it is that you had information that the HVO planned an attack on Prozor and that that was the reason for which you left your positions facing the Serbian army and you set off in the direction of Gornji Vakuf? Where did you have information of this alleged attack that the HVO was going to attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that statement was drafted a lot later. At that point in time when I was ordered to go towards Prozor, to the Lapsunj settlement, on the basis of the information of the HVO, I knew that positions would be taken there. I had information. I could use the phone freely. There was information according to which a lot of forces had massed in Prozor. The situation was apparently tense, and on that day, on the 22nd, the negotiations were under way that continued on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that your commander, Sabic, ordered you to leave the front line and to set off in the direction of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask him that, what he meant, but as the situation reached a head and they said that there was chaos reigning in Prozor, most of the time from June up until that date, 80 per cent of the day I spent in Idovac within different shifts. And I got on very well. Let me just give you an example to bear out what I'm saying. I think -- just half a minute. Half a minute. One minute. Can I just be allowed to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, if you need to say anything additionally, you can do so during the Prosecution time, whereas I would like to use my time for other things. In the documents that you referred to yesterday shown to you by the Prosecutor, there is in my mind certain contradictions with respect to the facilities that were shelled, with respect to the casualties, and with respect to the duration of the attack on Prozor. So I'd like to clear that up, clear the circumstances up. Now, with respect to the facilities targeted, what did the reports say that you were aware of since you weren't in Prozor yourself? What was targeted?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like to clarify what order is meant? What report is meant by the counsel? So that we could follow what is the question about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What report?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't think I need mention that because the Prosecution showed a large number of -- did not show a large number of documents, but it was P00744. And another exhibit P01656. Now, as far as the casualties were concerned, there was an additional document and it was P01542. So three documents in all, not many, where contradictory facts are stated. I don't think I need show the witness the documents. I'd like the witness to the best of his recollection to give us answers to the questions I ask him. And if those answers coincide with some of the information presented in the report, we'll move on and not waste any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, my question is as follows: Which facilities or buildings in the town of Prozor were shelled on that day, the 23rd or 24th of October, 1992? What buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, information received from the then commander of the headquarters of the staff and many refugees, the shells fell all over town, especially in those parts of town which were inhabited by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you receive information that certain facilities were special targets of attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Special targets of attack were places where the command was located, the Staff Command and certain parts of the Staff Command that were not all put up in the post office or fire brigade or cultural centre or whatever it was called, and in some parts of town where they had relocated. So that's what was shelled and targeted. And as the population did not expect anything like that, there was general chaos. All hell broke loose.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, what about residential buildings? Were residential buildings largely damaged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that because I didn't see them afterwards, so I can't say. But most probably some of the buildings had to be -- must have been destroyed, because afterwards, after the war, the centre or what did we call it, where the post office is now, the cultural centre or whatever, 500.000 Deutschmarks were spent to rebuild it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, without showing you the documents again, but of course we can if we need to do so, I would like -- if I say that in document P00744, which is a report on the situation in Prozor municipality dated the 14th of November, 1992, if I tell you that that report states that that there were no major damages to residential buildings. And that's on page 2 of the Croatian text and page 3 of the English text. And that in document number P01656, and that is the report on the situation in Prozor municipality dated the 12th of March, 1993, it is noted on page 9 of the Croatian text and 10 of the English text, and I quote: "That despite the shelling there were no major damages to residential buildings." Tell us now, please, whether these reports that I mentioned, and do you consider that -- them to be truthful and correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say. I didn't see those buildings at the time, so I can't say. But it is possible. It is possible that some of those buildings after that were devastated. Well, armies are very similar to each other. Whenever you get soldiers coming into a building, they do what they like, and it's -- you can't control it. You can agree with that or not, but that's how things stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since you have defined yourself as one of the co-authors of those reports, I assume that you're not challenging the correctness of the information in them. Now, as far as casualties are concerned, can you tell us whether during the night of that attack took place whether there were any civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not many. But the first information that received us because there was general chaos said that there were dozens of casualties. However, the total -- over those two days there were just seven or eight victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like us to show P01656 to the witness now, please, and page 9 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That will be the last question, because your time is up. You've already stepped over your time limit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be accorded the right to ask an additional question and then a concluding question? So that would make two additional questions, please. I don't think I'll make up too much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is the last question. This must be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, following on from what we were talking about a moment ago, may witness be shown page 9 of P01656, the Croatian text, that is. And page 10 of the English text. Because I don't have time, I'll just tell you that in the document, it is a report on the situation in Prozor municipality on the 12th of March, 1993. It says: "During the brutal attack there were no civilian casualties."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you say -- did I hear 20 March, 1993? That would be quite a time jump, because we were in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. It is a report which the Prosecution showed us with that number and that date, and then we have P00744. That's the other exhibit, where on page 2 the following was recorded, and I quote: "During that attack, there were no civilian casualties."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which attack, madam? Which attack?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which attack? On the 23rd or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We're just asking about a single attack, one single attack. And now my last question. How long did that attack last, days or hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Prozor started approximately, give or take five minutes, the 23rd at about 1525, or let's say 1530, and the conflicts ended at the end of the next day, the 24th, in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: During the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the 24th. They went on to the night of the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, my concluding question. Would you agree with me, then, that in the document that we saw yesterday, the document P01542, it was a request by Omer Hujdur, dated the 23rd of February, 1993, for defining the status, and in that document something is stated incorrectly, that the conflict, the shelling that we discussed a moment ago, was a bestial two-day shelling with the help of all available artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this report was written, that is to say in November, 1992, all the reports coming in from the refugees indicated -- led us to conclude that general chaos reigned in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the end of it. We have to stop there. Sit down. Who will be the next Defence team? How many more have we got for the cross-examination? For Mr. Prlic, you will have 25 minutes, and another 25 minutes, which makes it 50 minutes. It is now a quarter to 4.00 -- gone a quarter to 4.00. We're going to have a 15-minute break because we have one more witness. So we're going to have a 15-minute break and reconvene at approximately two minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First Defence team, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Suzana Tomanovic. I'm a lawyer from Bosnia-Herzegovina and I am a Defence counsel defending Dr. Jadranko Prlic here. I'd like you to answer as briefly as possible to my questions so I can conclude in the time allotted me by the Court. Since the two of us are fairly close to each other and my microphone can pick up your voice, if I notice that you have not understood my question, I'll give you a sign so that I can switch on and switch off my microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear your voice, but I can't hear you through the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll see what the problem is. Perhaps your headset isn't working properly. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we go into private session for a two minutes, please, first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few questions linked to the functioning of the Executive Board and the way in which decision-making took place. Since this is something that you know very well, you can just give me "yes" or "no" answers to my questions. The authority of the secretariat for defence was among others to implement the republican law on total national defences such as self-protection and the other bylaws related to that law.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it was enacted in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal Assembly also in conformity with this law was responsible for drafting provisions in the sphere of social self-protection and national defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could take decisions but it could not issue provisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just yes or no, please, and we'll get through this very quickly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's see what the procedure was like if the Municipal Assembly was supposed to bring in certain regulations from national defence. In the Secretariat for National Defence, for example, a draft decision would be compiled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to add a certain tense. I'm sorry. I have to say something more for it to be able to function there was the national defence alliance.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't need those details thank you. The secretary would send in its decision to the Executive Board for it's deliberation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: At its meeting the Executive Board would discuss the decision and then it would put it to the vote and the majority vote would pass the provision; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the votes in this case meant an absolute majority so one more than half the number of members in the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was regulated by the rules of procedure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now, if the Executive Board agreed with the text of the decision it would propose that the decision come up on the agenda for the next Municipal Assembly session; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly would then discuss the decision at its session and once again take a vote, the majority vote would mean that it would go through if not it would not go through is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: If the decision were adopted by majority vote, the president of the Municipal Assembly would sign it and it would then be published in the Official Gazette of the Municipal Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Executive Board was also in charge of making certain decisions in the sphere of total national defence; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: The procedure was the same. The Secretariat of National Defence would draft the text. It -- these would be sent to the Executive Board for debate and discussion, and the Executive Board once again would take a vote on whether to pass the decision or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that decision, the defence alliance would first of all discuss it and then the procedure would be as you have described it, but the defence council would first look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the interpreters heard your answer. Yes, they have. Anyway, that was the procedure. After that, the president of the Executive Board would sign a conclusion about the decision and depending on the degree of confidentiality of the document and this was regulated by a separate regulation, would either published the decision in the Official Gazette or not publish it if it was highly confidential?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was not confidential and secret on the basis of these provisions it would be published. Anything confidential would not be published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, there was a special rule and regulation dealing with what could be published in the Official Gazette and what could not be published.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it would in conformity with the state law that was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: So that republican law was in conformity with the state law.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to be, otherwise it couldn't function. And I think lawyers know that full well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the essence of decision-making in the Executive Board and in the Municipal Assembly was that a vote would be taken and the majority vote would prevail.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And -- but usually it was unanimous. The vote was unanimous.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: But it could also have been issued by out-voting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that's what the rules of procedure provided for.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We spoke about the time when there was a one-party system and the manner of voting in the administrative organs, assemblies, and Executive Committees in the municipalities. In 1990, the constitution was changed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: In order to make it possible to introduce a multi-party system, the election laws were changed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have an excerpt here from a book written by Mr. Suad Arnautovic entitled, Elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990. He analysed the voting or election process. Do you know who Suad Arnautovic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you briefly. He is a political scientist who graduated as such from university, and in 1995 and 1996 he was a lecturer at the University of Sarajevo. He was among a group of experts --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour. I cannot understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
