utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the importance of that, counsel? What relevance does it have?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We provided this document when Mr. Karnavas was supposed to cross-examine Mr. Tomljanovich, but we realised there was no point in presenting this document to (redacted) (redacted) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I allow you to continue, what are you trying to prove? What are you trying to demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour. It must be redacted. I mean, page 46, line 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was a big mistake. May we have that redacted. All the questions that you have raised, we find them in the rules. Now, what do you wish to demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to challenge point 26 of the indictment, and this count is listed in the proofing chart along with this witness. It says the HVO took control of [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] services removing or marginalising local Bosnian Muslim leaders. Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and forces to control over the media and enforce the Croatian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If I understand what you're saying, you wish to demonstrate that through elections the Croats took control of matters, is that right, in the municipality, the regular elections. Go ahead, ask him the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: We can have it in e-court. 1D00920. And while waiting for it to show up, I'll put a question to you. Mr. Suad Arnautovic on page 3 of his book and in e-court, that's page 3 in Croatian and page 3 in English, and I'll ask you whether you agree with this or not. In his book, he reached the following conclusion: "The elections were significantly determined by the mixed electoral system. The model and structure of the Presidency of the republic and the predetermined ethnic quotas and in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina according to certain formulas. These same elections were held simultaneously for local assemblies. And in the third paragraph in both languages on page 3 in e-court he says: "The electoral laws and other rules and regulations promoted a completely new and (old) political profile ethnic affiliation as a badge of political legitimacy. This law prescribed ethnic affiliation as a prerequisite in the electoral process for all organs and bodies in the republic. In other words, it is evident now that in these elections the voters of Bosnia and Herzegovina ceded their sovereignty as citizens to their national sovereignty." Do you agree with this statement by Mr. Arnautovic, who is now a member of the electoral commission for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he wrote it down, what does it matter whether I agree with it or not? I cannot influence anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to save time, the 1990 elections for Prozor, do you know the results of them? Because they're in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honours, I was just about to ask this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just ask -- wondering whether you were going to ask him that, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 14 in Croatian in e-court, and page 15 in the other language. In the English language it's 1D300135.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: You have here on the screen a table published by Mr. Arnautovic in his book, and you can find Prozor there. Can you see it? It's the fifth row. Do you see Prozor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Posusje, Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Under Prnjavor there's Prozor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see in this table of election results, there were 48 seats in the Prozor Assembly. Of these, the HDZ won 31 seats. The Party of Democratic Action won 14 seats and the League of Communists of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Socialist Democrat party won 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Social Democrats.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Social Democrats, yes. Now, there's something I'm interested in here. According to the census of 1991, in Prozor municipality, at least according to what is in the indictment, there were 62 per cent Croats, 33 per cent Muslims, and 2.5 per cent others.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many Muslims did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: 36.5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipality, not the town?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would be approximately the case, but --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's the census result, then it must be valid.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If we calculate the percentages and see how many seats each party won in the Assembly, we have 64.58 per cent for the HDZ, which is almost 3 per cent more than there were Croats in Prozor municipality. For the SDA, 14 places corresponds to 29.1 per cent, which is about 6 per cent less than the number of Muslims in the municipality. And the 3 seats won by the League of Communists would correspond to some 6.25 per cent. Can we conclude from this that in Prozor municipality people who were not ethnic Croats also voted for the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'll explain this. I was directly involved in verifying the electoral lists for these elections. In these -- the electoral register, that is. And many Croats who did not reside in Prozor municipality but originated from the municipality voted. These people moved out after the Rama power electric -- hydroelectric power plant was built. I'm a hundred per cent certain of this. But as this is an official report --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss these details most probably with an expert.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not interested in that. That's the past.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in now is the following: The electoral system changed, but the manner of reaching decisions in the organs of government and the authorities remained the same. It was an absolute majority that decided; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: With 31 seats in the Assembly, the HDZ did not need to enter into a coalition with any party. They could always have both an absolute and a relative majority, and they could have adopted most decisions without the participation of any other party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement on page 2 -- in your statement on page 2, you comment on this manner of adopting decisions. You seem to have felt that it was not fair that the Croats, through the HDZ, issued most of the decisions, although there were 37 per cent Muslims in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But it's true that all decisions were made in the way the HDZ wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: But that was the existing system. That was what the constitution provided for. Nothing could be done differently; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's why things were as they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this kind of system where there is one man, one vote, cannot be the appropriate solution for multi-ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view the current electoral law is no good either.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you about the system that existed then. Did you feel it was fair or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't think it was fair then, and I don't think it's fair now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to hear that the basic demand of the representatives of the Croats in all the negotiations at the international level after the outbreak of the war was that they did not want a unitary state where decision-making would proceed according to the same system, one man, one vote? The Croats were a constituent nation, and they had only 17.5 per cent of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they felt that this kind of electoral system, this kind of voting and decision-making unfair; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they know whether they felt that way or not; I don't. But in my view, I would change the electoral law if I could, but the Croats probably wouldn't like my law either.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the Croats were right in asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Time's up. No more questions. We'll move on to the next Defence team. We have to be very strict when it comes to time. The next Defence team has 25 minutes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. I am an attorney at law from Zagreb. And in these proceedings, I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Valentin Coric. In view of the nature of my questions which will be brief, can we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're in open session -- yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to tender the two documents. May I do that now? Thank you, Your Honour. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution wishes to tender the statement of Witness BN, and it is available under the number P09700, and the section document is P08268. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence counsel, you are asking if there are any documents to be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, my apologies. May I also request that these two documents remain under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak's Defence, as you requested, we can read out all the exhibits that concern the previous witness BM, and one document concerning the last one, the last witness, BN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's first deal with Witness BN, with this witness. Could we have the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the last witness, we have only one document, 3D00422.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we admit into evidence P09700, P08268, and 3D00422. And now for the previous witness. First the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. The Prosecution would tender the following documents which were shown to the witness BM P00640, P00657, P00744, P01188, P01542, P01656, P02180, P09376, P09429, P09482, P09487, P09694, and P09702 which we would request be placed under seal. That is only the last exhibit under seal, P09702. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just one thing. As far as the numbers for the previous P09700 and 3D0042 are under seal of course. Yes, and now Defence counsel. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Stojic's Defence wants to tender two documents, 2D00054, and 2D00148. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And for the next Defence team now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Praljak's Defence would like to tender the following documents for the previous witness. The first document used was 3D00291, which has already been tendered into evidence. So it's not necessary to repeat. Then we have 3D00418, which was used a day earlier. It was marked for identification at the time, so we now want to tender it again. Then we have 3D00419, 3D00420. This document has also been marked for identification because it was tendered a day earlier and a decision wasn't rendered at the time. Then we have 3D00290. We'd rather have 3D00419 used as number for this document. Ms. Pinter produced this document. It also bears the stamp of the Croatian state archives whereas 3D00290 is an identical copy of the document but it doesn't have the stamp. That's why we'd rather have the number 419 for this document. Then we have document 3D00289. This was earlier admitted as an exhibit. And then we have P00898. A day earlier it was used. It was marked for identification. And then we have three documents that General Praljak placed on the ELMO today. They're in the e-court system under 3D00423, under that number, and under 3D00424, and 3D00425. And perhaps I should just briefly describe the documents as they were on the ELMO. The first one, 423, is dated the 25th of October, 1992. It's a message from the ABiH from the person called Tetak. 424, the second document, is dated the 14th of November, 1992. It's an order that mentions the seizure of a vehicle in the municipality of Prozor. It was signed by Praljak and Coric. The last document 425 is a document dated the 30th of November, 1992. It is an order signed by the accused Coric. As far as this number is concerned, it was P00898. It was in the transcript a minute ago. I must make a correction. 889 is the correct number, P00889. And those are all the documents that Mr. Praljak's Defence would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that when Mr. Praljak commenced his examination he showed a map where one could see a corridor, the direction of movement. This map seemed very interesting to me. You are not requesting that this document be admitted into evidence? We don't have a number for that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we'd like to tender this into evidence, but since it was prepared by the Defence as -- as a document that could assist us when we cross-examine witnesses, we hadn't intended to tender it into evidence but we would be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you could do so next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. If you have any desires, Your Honours, we'd be very interested in using such maps with such witnesses, with these kind of witnesses. You also mentioned the fact, but it seems we haven't found a technical solution for this for the moment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And now for the next Defence team. Are there any requests in that case? I thank you. Yes, go ahead Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender the following: 1 -- 1D00920. This is Mr. Arnautovic's book on the elections in Bosnia and Hercegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which page exactly? Pursuant to our decision, it is necessary to indicate the pages or paragraphs. Because we're not going to admit the entire book into evidence. Okay about the elections. Very well then, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a complete series. P09702 is another document I'd like to tender into evidence. It's a witness statement we were promised, an amended version with the correct names, but we haven't received it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that all? Very well thank you. No more requests? Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one other matter if I could raise it briefly. I would apply for a brief extension of time within which to file a response regarding -- or a document regarding the documents produced or referred to by the witness Mr. Tomljanovich. Your Honour's present order is that we should file it by the end of this week which I take to be tomorrow. Your Honour, I would like some further time to confer with my colleagues on this matter. In particular, Mr. Karnavas has not been here this week as Your Honours have even. If we could have until Tuesday. I don't think any prejudice would be caused to the Prosecution by that. I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your request shall be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as next week is concerned. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was just passed a note by my case manager whose efficiency always amazes me. With respect to Witness BM, I missed one Prosecution Exhibit which was P01425 and we would ask that be admitted. That was another document which was shown to Witness BM. With respect to next week, Your Honours, Monday through Wednesday we have Witness BA, that's Bravo Alpha, who will testify. Mr. Scott earlier submitted a letter to the Defence counsel with a copy to the Chamber's legal officer informing everyone that we would offer much of Witness BA's evidence by way of her written statement, in order to expedite things and so that there is sufficient time for the Defence to cross-examine that witness. Mr. Scott also indicated in his letter that he anticipates, barring any unforeseen developments, he anticipates completing or concluding the examination-in-chief of Witness BA by Monday afternoon leaving Tuesday and Wednesday for questions from the Defence and/or Your Honours. And then we have following that witness -- we have a witness scheduled for Thursday of next week who -- that would be Witness number 269 on the Prosecution exhibit list. This is the witness that was previously listed for September 28. That witness will be appearing and testifying on Thursday of next week. So we have Witness BA Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, followed by the witness listed as number 269 on the Prosecution's 65 ter list and that should take us through a full week of witness testimony for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Witness BA is concerned, if I am understanding this correctly, you would like to use the procedure that comes under Rule 89(F). You'll be asking for his written statement to be tendered, and you will examine him with regard to the documents, and then on Tuesday and Wednesday we'll have time for the cross-examination. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. -- as I indicated, Mr. Scott will be dealing with this witness, but my understanding is that we will be predominantly relying on the written witness statement of the witness, but perhaps, asking a few questions concerning certain parts of that written statement so that that evidence can be led viva voce. But again, there are a number of documents and those documents will be the primary subject matter that Mr. Scott will be dealing with with the witness. And again, we believe that with two days of cross-examination, there should be adequate opportunity for the witness's credibility and other matters to be tested when Witness BA appears in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Initially, if you had conducted your cross-examination for Witness BA, how much time would you have needed or how much time would you need if you were to conduct your examination-in-chief for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honours, that we had initially indicated 3.5 hours for a full direct examination of Witness BA. I -- I'm looking, as I speak, at the calendar that was provided, and that indicates 3.5 hours. I don't recall if that number matches what was on the 65 ter list or not. As a general rule, the calendar times match the 65 ter list but not always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as Thursday's witness is concerned, how much time had you planned on using? Because we have to determine how much time the Defence has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I anticipate with the witness on Thursday that we will be taking two hours or slightly less time than that. I am endeavouring to try to get the direct examination of that witness down to one 90-minute court session so that by the end -- by the first break on Thursday, hopefully, hopefully, I'll be done with the direct examination of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you complete your examination before the first break on Thursday, it means the Defence will have almost the exact amount of time after the break. Ms. Pinter -- I apologise. As you are both blonde, that's why I confused your identities.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the -- as far as Monday's witness is concerned, if you have a look at her summary statement, if you have a look at the proofing chart, the witness talks about the joint criminal enterprise. It goes to the heart of the indictment. It concerns, above all, the alleged responsibility of my client, Dr. Prlic, his responsibilities for the events he is charged with in the indictment. So to summarise her statement has no justification since he has the right to a fair trial and to cross-examination of this witness. So we object to tendering into evidence any part of her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there is no summary. The Prosecution believes that the Defence will have two days, and they apparently won't be using the entire day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I have understood, they want to tender parts of her statement into evidence rather than have her direct testimony. If I have misunderstood something, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that Ms. Tomanovic has misunderstood. Mr. President, as we expressed yesterday when this issue arose, was that this is a mechanism, whether it be the old 89(F) or the new 92 ter, these are mechanisms for expediting the introduction of evidence before Your Honours. By taking less time with the witness's direct examination and tendering her written statement into evidence, more time is made available for cross-examination by the Defence teams given the limited amount of time that is available for this witness's overall testimony. So that -- so that our position -- the Prosecution position, let's be very clear about this with respect to all the remaining 92 ter witnesses that we call, whether we lead parts of their evidence viva voce and tender their written statement into evidence or whether we rely entirely upon their written statement pursuant to 92 ter, as long as sufficient time is provided for cross-examination, there should be no hindrance to that type of procedure. The less time the Prosecution takes on its direct, the more time is available for the Defence to cross-examine the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I wonder whether we have really a substance for dispute, because you have said, Mr. Mundis, that you would need for direct three and a half hours. You have already said that by proceeding the way you proposed, you would finish by Monday evening. Now, Monday afternoon's session amply covers three and a half hours, so I fail to see the interest in departing unless your three and a half hours are not serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are of course a number of factors that -- that can affect the time that we estimate. We estimate three and a half hours. That does not -- that estimate -- when those estimates were made does not envision any objections, any interventions by the Defence. To be quite open and transparent, those estimates did not include any time where Your Honours may intervene to ask questions of clarification, et cetera, so that our three and a half hour estimate of direct examination is three and a half hours of Prosecution direct examination time. Our experiences have shown, and I believe the numbers kept by the registry would bear this out, that three and a half hours of direct examination time tends to be much longer than three and a half hours of real running time. So if we were to take three and a half hours of direct examination as the counting mechanism has been used in this case, that would take us well into Tuesday, thereby cutting into the amount of time that's available for the Defence teams. To be honest and transparent, that seems to be the experience, and we've been tracking these numbers quite carefully for these very purposes. So that what we're trying to do is to ensure that the Defence have adequate time to cross-examine, and that means cutting down the amount of time we spend, while at the same time, meeting our duties and obligations will require us at times to tender the statement but also ask questions about certain parts of the statements as well as the documents that we think the witness is in a position to testify about in order to get those documents into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. To respond to what was said a minute ago, we rendered a decision on the duration of cross-examination. You know that the Defence should have the same amount of time as the Prosecution when we're talking about base crimes, and when we're dealing with joint criminal enterprise, we have decided that the Defence will have 50 per cent additional time. According to these calculations, if you have two days, Tuesday and Wednesday, you have even more time than that, so I don't see why you should complain. Now, if you're worried about Mr. Prlic's situation, it's up to you to reach an agreement with your colleagues, and you can perhaps take all the time for you to reach an agreement. We won't be sitting -- or we don't sit on Fridays, and this allows the Defence teams to meet and to discuss the strategy that they will employ to discuss how they will act in future, and it also allows you to see your clients and to plan for the weeks to come. It's up to you to reach agreements, and if you fail to reach an agreement, you must inform us of the fact and then the Judges will decide, but the Judges would prefer you to reach agreements. With regard to certain witnesses, yes, perhaps one Defence team might take up most of the time and then the other Defence teams might use up the rest of the time. This could be done if you reach an agreement, but if not, it will be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand what you are saying, and I must say that I'm grateful to all of my colleagues, because we often grant the other Defence teams our time, and they do the same when it is useful. However, the time we need for cross-examination -- well, we'll need more time if part of a statement is introduced into evidence. If two pages are introduced into evidence, for example, because you have a lot more information in two pages than when you have 15 minutes of examination. So the question is how much time is adequate for cross-examination? We have raised this issue a number of times. It concerns introducing a hundred pages of transcript as evidence, for example. That's what's at stake. We don't have any problems when it comes to reaching agreements, but what is important is how much documents are tendered and whether we have sufficient time for cross-examination given the documents tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're not going to start debating a decision that has already been rendered. A decision has been rendered, and going back to the matter is out of the question. But I personally can say that on the basis of my experience in the last few months, sometimes the cross-examination is very interesting and very relevant, and sometimes the questions, the purpose of which one fails to understand. Perhaps we're not seeing the entire picture, but sometimes one wonders what you are trying to prove. So try to make a distinction between what is essential and what is of secondary importance. You certainly have a certain objective, but it's necessary to explain your objective to us. As an example, you put some questions about the elections. These are problems we are familiar with because the subject has already been raised, but before putting the question it's better to tell us, "I'm going to put a question about the elections," and then we'll understand your objective. Otherwise, we're here. We'll listen to you. And we wonder what you're trying to prove and in fact sometimes we feel that time is being wasted. I know it's difficult, but you should be aware of the fact that your questions must be of use to us. We have to render a reasoned judgement, and the reasons must be based not only on oral information but on documents too. And this goes to the issue of responsibility with regard to what happened. I'm not going to mention anyone, but when we go back to the question of the interviews between or agreements or discussions between Milosevic and Tudjman, all that's very interesting. We have already addressed this matter. We've had experts here. But in the course of cross-examination, we re-address such issues, and I then wonder why. Perhaps there is a reason. But very often you put questions to witnesses that have already been asked. Perhaps with time this will improve. This will certainly improve with time. So as far as the duration of cross-examination is concerned, we have rendered a decision and it's necessary to abide by that decision. We have to be very strict because unfortunately we have time limitations and our main concerns go to the heart of the matter, to the heart of the problems, and to do so sometimes we have to take very complicated routes, but if you want to take complicated routes to go to the heart of the matter you have to explain this to us so we can understand better why you're asking certain questions in the course of your cross-examination. I'd like to thank you. This completes today's hearing. You should meet on Friday to discuss all these problems and to see your clients. I hope that Mr. Pusic will be back here on Monday. So I will see you all on Monday at 1415, but you should know that the week after we'll be having hearings in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
